title: Pull requests
idea: On GitHub, a pull request asks a project's maintainers to merge your branch into their repository. Without write access, you work from a fork: your own copy.

analogy.text: Suggesting a change to a cookbook someone else owns: you photocopy it, mark your edits on the copy, then hand the owner a note asking them to adopt it.
analogy.breaks: The note starts a discussion, and you can keep adding edits to it.

points: Clone your fork; Git names that remote `origin`. Add the original, say as `upstream`.
Work on a new branch, commit, and push that branch to `origin`.
On GitHub, open a pull request from your branch into the original's `main`.
Reviewers comment. Push more commits to the same branch, and the request updates.

steps.caption: The original repository belongs to its maintainers. Without write access, you cannot push to it.
Forking copies it into your own account on GitHub. You can push to your fork.
You clone your fork to your laptop. Git names that remote `origin`.
On a new branch, `fix-readme`, you commit B and push the branch to `origin`.
You open a pull request: a proposal to merge `fix-readme` into the original's `main`. Nothing merges yet.
Reviewers comment. You push another commit, C, to the same branch, and the open request picks it up.
A maintainer merges the request. The original now holds your changes.
Later, other work lands in the original as D. Your fork and clone do not move until you sync them.
`git fetch upstream` downloads D. Merge it into your local `main`.
`git push origin main` updates your fork on GitHub. All three copies match.

code.title: Fork, branch, sync
code.caption: Real Git output. Bare repositories on disk play the original and your fork; the pull request itself happens on GitHub.

walk.text: Create the maintainers' project with one commit.
Two bare copies play GitHub's part: `upstream.git` is the original, `fork.git` is your fork.
Clone your fork. Git names its URL `origin`.
Add the original as a second remote, `upstream`. `remote -v` lists both.
Branch, commit, then push the branch to your fork. On GitHub you would now open the pull request.
Meanwhile the maintainers add a commit to the original.
Fetch the original, fast-forward `main` to it, and push to update your fork.

pitfalls: Branch for each change; commits on your fork's `main` make syncing it harder.
Read the project's `CONTRIBUTING.md`, if it has one, before you start.
Keep each pull request to one change; small ones are easier to review.

quiz.q: What does the last command print?
quiz.code:
# on main, in sync with origin (your fork);
# upstream has gained one new commit
git fetch upstream
git status -sb
quiz.why: `main` tracks `origin`, your fork, not `upstream`. Fetching `upstream` updates `upstream/main` only, so your fork still looks up to date.

takeaway: Branch in your fork, push it, then propose the merge with a pull request.

starters: Do I need a fork if I have write access?
How do I keep my fork up to date?
What should a good pull request description say?
